issues.explanation: 'People cycling' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile for a refugee trauma presentation when the other triggers are funerals/graves and car sounds, and there are no corresponding memory or appraisal items suggesting bicycles or a cycling-related trauma cue. This trigger looks clinically disconnected from the stated trauma context and the rest of the network.

'I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. In an older married male refugee with severe PTSD symptoms, self-harm can occur, but here it is the only extreme behavioral regulation item and is unsupported by the other selected strategies, memories, or appraisals. It appears clinically out of pattern relative to the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation.

# Rajesh's Burden

Rajesh Kumar had spent fifty-three years turning clay into vessels—bowls that held water, plates that held food, cups that held tea shared between friends. His hands knew the weight and give of the material so completely that he could work with his eyes closed, feeling the subtle resistance as the wheel spun, reading the clay's moisture in the tension at his fingertips. At seventy-five, his studio in Portland remained his sanctuary, the one place where time moved in the rhythm of his own breathing and the hum of the kiln. But that sanctuary had begun to feel like a cage, and the hands that had always known what to do had become unreliable instruments of a mind he no longer recognized.

The trauma that shaped Rajesh lived in fragments he could not assemble. In 1971, when he was twenty-three, the war came to East Pakistan—what would become Bangladesh—and his family's neighborhood became a place of sudden, incomprehensible violence. He remembered the sound of vehicles, the urgent shouting of men in uniform, the way his mother's hand gripped his shoulder so hard it left marks. He remembered running, the smell of smoke, the feeling of being separated from his older brother in a crowd. Beyond that, his mind offered only disconnected pieces: a glimpse of a truck bed, the sensation of being shoved, a woman's scream he could never quite place. The memory did not cohere into a narrative he could tell; it remained fragmented, existing more as a visceral storm of sensation than as a story with a beginning and end. What he could say with certainty was that he had survived, that his brother had not, and that he had spent the next five decades trying to build a life that honored that arbitrary mercy.

The first real symptom appeared two years ago, after his neighbor's funeral. Rajesh had attended out of respect, but standing at the graveside, he felt something crack open inside him. The sight of the coffin being lowered, the finality of it, the way the earth was thrown in—all of it felt not like a single moment but like every loss he had ever experienced collapsing into one. He left the cemetery shaking, unable to speak for hours. Since then, funerals had become impossible. His wife Priya received the invitations; she attended alone. When she mentioned that their dear friend Ashok had passed, or that the temple was holding a memorial service, Rajesh felt his chest tighten. He had come to believe that his presence at such events would somehow cause harm, that his grief was too large and too dangerous to contain in the presence of others' sorrow. The cemetery triggered not just sadness but a deep conviction that he was no longer capable of bearing the weight of life's sorrows—that he had already used up whatever reserves of strength he possessed in simply surviving the war.

The car sounds began around the same time. A siren wailing past the house, the aggressive honk of a horn in traffic, the sudden rev of an engine—each sound catapulted Rajesh back to that moment of shouting and vehicles, though he could not articulate why. His body reacted before his mind could catch up, his heart racing, his muscles tensing as though he needed to run. The memory itself remained wordless and scattered, a chaos of sensation rather than a clear picture, but the sounds seemed to unlock something in him that knew danger. When a police car pulled up to the neighbor's house one evening (a false alarm, a misunderstanding), Rajesh watched from behind the living room curtain, his hands trembling, certain in a way he could not explain that authority and violence were inseparable.

Over the past eighteen months, Rajesh had begun to organize his life around the avoidance of these triggers. He stopped attending community events where he might encounter grief or loss. He declined invitations to dinners, to temple functions, to the pottery guild's summer exhibition—anything that might make him feel hopeful or connected, because hope felt dangerous, a kind of hubris that invited punishment. When Priya suggested they take a trip to visit their grandson in Seattle, he found reasons to refuse: the drive was too long, his knees were bothering him, perhaps next year. The real reason was that the thought of being away from home, in an unfamiliar place, felt impossible. He could not predict what he might encounter; he could not control the sounds or the spaces. It was safer to stay, to keep his world small.

This shrinking began to feed on itself. The less Rajesh did, the more convinced he became that he was incapable of doing anything. His wife had always been the peacemaker in their marriage, and he had grown accustomed to deferring to her in social decisions. But now he found himself unable to engage in even mild disagreement with her—about what to watch on television, about how to spend an afternoon. Any hint of conflict sent him spiraling into a state of vigilance, scanning for threats that existed only in his mind, certain that discord would escalate into something he could not survive. He began checking the locks on the doors repeatedly, counting them sometimes five or six times before bed. He would sit in his workshop and listen to the street outside, identifying each sound—a car, a truck, footsteps, a child's voice—as though cataloging a landscape of potential danger.

The pottery itself became impossible. Rajesh would sit at the wheel, his hands positioned as they had been ten thousand times before, and feel nothing but paralysis. The clay felt foreign, resistant. His mind would fragment the task into impossible components: the pressure of his fingers, the speed of the wheel, the risk of the piece collapsing. He had come to believe that he no longer possessed the steady hands or the calm mind that pottery required. What had once felt like meditation now felt like a test he was certain to fail. He stopped going to the studio. For a man whose identity had been built on the ability to transform raw material into beauty, this loss was not incidental—it was a kind of death in itself.

Priya had begun to notice the changes months ago, but it was only last week, when she found Rajesh sitting in the dark at three in the morning, his breathing shallow and rapid, unable to articulate what had frightened him, that she insisted he see someone. The sounds of a late-night delivery truck outside had triggered something—not a memory exactly, but a cascade of disconnected sensations and certainties: that danger was imminent, that he was powerless, that the world was fundamentally unsafe in ways he could never explain to anyone who had not lived through what he had lived through. He came to the appointment because Priya had made it, because he loved her, and because some small part of him wondered if there might be a way to reclaim the man he used to be—the one who could hold clay in his hands and know exactly what to do with it.
